title: Pine wells: depth, yield and drilling cost
meta_description: Pine-area wells have a 305-foot median depth and 5.0 gpm median yield. See local drilling costs, water levels and checks before buying.
h1: What to expect from a well near Pine
intro_html:
A well near Pine is a fractured-bedrock job, not a predictable groundwater target. Local records show a median depth of 305 feet, but the middle half runs from 200 to 500 feet. That spread matters when you price a lot or compare drilling bids.

This guide covers Colorado DWR permit records within 5 miles of Pine in Park County. There are 8,242 permit records, with 5,639 recorded as constructed. Use these figures as a neighborhood reference, then look closely at wells around the actual parcel. Nearby Bailey and Conifer provide local context, but a nearby address does not guarantee the same drilling conditions.

sections.heading: Pine's bedrock makes depth a budget variable
sections.html:
Among the 5,826 wells reporting depth, the median is 305 feet. The middle half falls between 200 and 500 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 700 feet. A bid built around the median needs a clear price for continuing deeper; 305 feet is a planning reference, not a stopping point that guarantees water.

The permit descriptions are dominated by unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with Fractured Crystalline and Fractured Granite also listed. Water comes from connected fractures in the mountain rock. Their location and productivity can change across a parcel. Compare nearby completion logs, particularly around the proposed drilling location, rather than assuming wells toward Bailey or Conifer establish your depth.

sections.heading: A 5.0 gpm well still needs a demand plan
sections.html:
The 3,231 reported pump yields have a 5.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 2.0 and 7.2 gpm. That is useful planning information for household supply, but a reported pump yield is not a guarantee of sustained output through changing conditions.

7% report less than 1 gpm. For a buyer, that is a reason to make a current pumping and recovery test part of due diligence, rather than accepting that a working faucet proves adequate supply. A low-producing well may need storage and careful demand management. A deeper hole does not automatically produce more water in fractured rock. Also check permitted uses: 94% of the records are domestic/household, but the individual permit controls what is allowed.

sections.heading: Water at 85 feet does not mean an 85-foot well
sections.html:
Only 395 records report a static water level. Their median is 85 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 42 and 184 feet. Static level describes where water rests when the well is not pumping; it is not the total drilled depth or the pumping level under demand.

The decade medians do not show a steady decline in the water table. They move from 40 feet in the 1960s to 120 in the 1990s, back to 52 in the 2000s, then 120 in the 2010s and 98 in the 2020s. These are measurements from different wells, not a continuous monitoring record. Ask for repeat measurements and recovery information on the property itself.

sections.heading: Pine's drilling record is largely an older one
sections.html:
Permit issuance was strongest in the 1990s, with 2,129 permits, followed by 1,917 in the 1970s. The records include 258 permits from the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025. Permits document authorization and history; they do not establish that every listed well was completed or remains serviceable.

The most represented drillers are Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert), with 1,045 records; Stan'S Drilling (Stansbury, Larry), with 622; and James Drilling Company (Keaton, Michael K.), with 478. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. On an existing Pine property, use the permit and completion documents to identify who drilled it and what was actually installed.

sections.heading: Budgeting a new well in Pine's granite and gneiss
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $65-$100 per foot for drilling fractured mountain bedrock. At the 305-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $19,800-$30,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $25,800-$42,500.

Treat that as a planning range, not a parcel-specific quote. The 200-500-foot middle depth range leaves substantial room for the drilling bill to move. Have the contractor spell out casing, grout, testing, mobilization and what happens if drilling must continue. Steep access, a difficult rig setup and the route from the well to the house can affect the scope. Compare bids with the same finished-system requirements.

sections.heading: Check water quality and the buildable layout together
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, the map identifies 5 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 20 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. Those markers warrant a closer look, but they do not prove that a particular Pine well is contaminated. A sampling location is not necessarily a confirmed contamination source.

Get property-specific laboratory testing and discuss additional testing with the lab or local health authority based on nearby site records. Inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage. Fractured rock also carries low-yield and dry-hole risk; local depth alone cannot settle either concern. Before fixing the house location, confirm a workable well site, septic layout, required separation distances and drilling access. A favorable water test does not resolve a constrained building layout.

sections.heading: Before closing on a Pine lot or well-served home
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit, not the listing's description of the well. Confirm the authorized uses, locate the completion report and match the paperwork to the physical well. For an existing home, obtain a current pumping and recovery test, laboratory results and available pump-service records.

For vacant land, review neighboring wells around the proposed site before committing to a drilling budget. The 305-foot median depth and 5.0 gpm median yield are reference points, not promises. Settle access, septic feasibility and permit eligibility early. Do not assume a household-use permit allows outdoor watering or livestock; expanded uses may require a different legal arrangement, including augmentation where applicable. Make unresolved water and site questions part of purchase due diligence.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Pine, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Pine, wells reporting depth have a median of 305 feet. The middle half ranges from 200 to 500 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 700 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes depth variable, so neighboring completion logs help with budgeting but cannot guarantee the depth needed on your parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Pine?
faq.a: The Pine cost model uses $65-$100 per foot for fractured-bedrock drilling. At the 305-foot median depth, the hole alone is about $19,800-$30,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $25,800-$42,500. Ask for a written scope covering casing, grout, access and the price of drilling deeper.

faq.q: How much water do wells near Pine produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields near Pine have a 5.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 2.0 and 7.2 gpm. Below 1 gpm accounts for 7% of reports. Before buying, get a current pumping and recovery test. Historical yield helps screen a property, but sustained supply and household peak demand still need evaluation.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Pine, Colorado?
faq.a: Permit records cannot establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles of Pine, mapped records include 5 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 20 historic mine features and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. Proximity does not prove contamination. Obtain property-specific laboratory testing and review nearby environmental records with the lab or local health authority when selecting additional tests.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Pine?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady drop. Static water levels were 120 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 98 feet in the 2020s, with substantial earlier fluctuations. Only 395 records report static levels, and these are not repeat measurements of the same wells. Evaluate the property's own water-level and recovery history.
